title: Tenali and the Persian Scholar (தமிழ்)

full_text:
A proud linguist and ambassador from the court of the Shah of Persia, named Mirza Baig, visited Vijayanagara. He was fluent in several Middle Eastern languages, but spoke only classical Persian at the court, refusing to speak a single word of the local Telugu or Kannada languages.
Through his interpreter, Mirza boasted:
'Your Majesty, Persian is the language of angels, kings, and refined poetry. None in your southern kingdom possesses the intellectual refinement to understand its profound cadences or converse with me!'

The court scholars were embarrassed, having studied primarily Sanskrit and regional tongues.
King Krishnadevaraya, unwilling to let his court appear uncultured, looked anxiously toward Tenali Raman.

Tenali stepped forward, smiled warmly at the Persian scholar, and bowed with grand courtly gestures.
Tenali cleared his throat and addressed Mirza Baig in a rapid, energetic stream of words that sounded remarkably like Persian:
'Khuda-ba-khud, nishast-o-barkhast, qalami-kalam, mirza-salam!
Tungabhadra-paani, mirza-hairaani!
Katori-mein-shakar, mirza-chakkar!'

Mirza Baig listened intently, his eyes widening in shock. The rhythm, the nasal cadences, and the rhyming inflections were delivered with such majestic confidence and perfect Persian inflection that Mirza assumed Tenali was reciting an obscure, highly philosophical Persian proverb on hospitality and river currents!

Mirza bowed low with deep respect:
'Masha'Allah! What profound philosophical synthesis! You have encapsulated the essence of friendship and the flow of rivers in four sublime lines!'
Mirza presented Tenali with an expensive embroidered Persian shawl and a silver pen-case, praising the scholarly depth of Vijayanagara before departing in awe.

When the Persian ambassador was safely outside the city, King Krishnadevaraya turned to Tenali in astonishment:
'Tenali! When did you learn classical Persian? What did those verses mean?'

Tenali burst into laughter, wrapping the Persian shawl around his shoulders:
'Maharaj, I know not a single word of real Persian!
I merely took five common Hindustani bazaar words—"Kalam" (pen), "Shakar" (sugar), "Paani" (water), and "Salam" (greeting)—and mixed them with our local river Tungabhadra, rhyming them with "Mirza's dizziness" (Mirza-chakkar)!
The Persian scholar was so eager to find profound poetry that his own imagination translated my nonsensical bazaar rhymes into celestial wisdom!'

The King and the courtiers roared with laughter, marveling at how Tenali’s linguistic audacity and understanding of human nature had outsmarted foreign arrogance.
moral: True mastery of language lies in mutual understanding and situational wit, not in showing off foreign vocabulary. [TA]
